raw_segments.text: Svidrigalov came to himself, got up from the bed and went to the window. He felt for the
latch and opened it. The wind lashed furiously into the little room and stung his face and
his chest, only covered with his shirt, as though with frost. Under the window there
must have been something like a garden, and apparently a pleasure garden. There, too,
probably there were tea tables and singing in the daytime.
Now drops of rain flew in at the window from the trees and bushes. It was dark as an acellar,
so that he could only just make out some dark blurs of objects. Svidrigalov, bending down with
elbows on the windowsill, gazed for five minutes into the darkness. The boom of a cannon,
followed by a second one, resounded in the darkness of the night. Ah, the signal! The
river is overflowing, he thought. By morning it will be swirling down the street in the lower
parts, flooding the basements and cellars. The cellar rats will swim out, and men will curse
in the rain and wind as they drag their rubbish to their upper stories. What time is it now?
